newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Iran's Velayati to tackle Gulf security in Kuwait.
newsitem.headline: Iran's Velayati to tackle Gulf security in Kuwait.

text.p: Iranian Foreign Minister Ali Akbar Velayati arrived in Kuwait on Monday where he is expected to discuss security in the oil-rich Gulf region.
The Iranian minister, on a 10-nation tour, will also deliver an invitation to Kuwait to attend the Organisation of the Islamic Conference (OIC) summit in Tehran in December.
Velayati has extended invitations to the summit to Saudi Arabia, Oman and Qatar.

Western diplomats said Velayati, on his fourth visit to Kuwait since the 1991 Gulf War, was expected to tackle a variety of issues, including growing concern with non-Arab Iran's arms procurement programme.
Velayati is trying to use his regional tour to clear some of the mistrust between Iran and its Gulf Arab neighbours and assure them that Tehran was not a potential threat, they said.
Iran's relations are often tense with its Arab neighbours across the Gulf who have accused it of interfering in their internal affairs. Iran denies the charges.

Kuwait, which backed Baghdad politically and financially during the 1980-88 Iran-Iraq war, has improved ties with Tehran which took a neutral stand during the 1990-91 Gulf crisis. Kuwait and its oil exporting tankers were often the target of Iranian attacks in the 1980s.

Velayati reiterated in comments in both Riyadh and Muscat his country's opposition to the role of U.S. and Western forces in the Gulf, saying that the security of the area was the responsibility of regional states.
"We think that the security of this sensitive region should be in the hands of its countries," Velayati told reporters in Muscat.
"But this cannot be achieved without positive cooperation among the countries of the region through the creation of a positive atmosphere on the basis of mutual understanding."

Iran has repeatedly condemned the U.S. military presence in the region, where U.S.-led forces enforce U.N. sanctions against Iraq. Iran says U.S. troops in the region, including about 5,000 in Saudi Arabia, increase regional tension.

Last month Iran warned Gulf Arab states with Western ties that they would be the first to "burn" if the region became instable. Washington accuses Iran and Iraq of trying to control the region's oil -- more than 60 percent of the world's proven reserves.

Iran's ambassador to Kuwait, GholamAli Sanati, told Reuters last month that the tiny Gulf Arab state had assured Tehran it would not let Washington use its territory in case of a military clash with the Islamic republic.
